speaker: wren
lines: You're Nana's Pip. She said you'd come up the valley before the snow.
I'm Wren. I write what the valley sounds like: springs, ice, pines knocking.
The book's nearly full. One page left, and nothing worth putting on it.

speaker: wren
lines: It's not the page. It's me. Everything sounds like something I've already written.
My very first page was the mast on Brindle Peak, humming in the cold. I was younger than you.

speaker: wren
lines: So listen for me. Fresh ears. Go to the hoarfrost glade and take a photograph.
Holding still for a picture is the only time anyone really listens. You'll hear the frost.
Then go down to Kettle Springs and walk in among the hot pools. Nothing sounds like that water. You'll hear it as you go.
Then come back and tell me what you heard. I'll put it on the last page.

speaker: wren
lines: You're back. The hoarfrost glade first. Hold still for the picture, and listen.
Then walk in among the hot pools at Kettle Springs, and listen. Then come and tell me.

speaker: wren
lines: The glade first, for the frost. Then the hot pools at Kettle Springs. Then me.

speaker: wren
lines: You've been to both. Go on, then. What did you hear?

choices.text: the frost ticked. like a stove cooling.
the springs. like a kettle arguing with itself.

speaker: wren
lines: A stove cooling. Oh, that's it exactly. I'd stopped hearing it.
And the springs? No, keep that one. I'll go down and hear it for myself.

speaker: wren
lines: A kettle arguing with itself. Oh, that's it exactly. I'd stopped hearing it.
And the frost? No, keep that one. I'll go up to the glade and listen for myself.

speaker: wren
lines: That's the last page. The book's full.
Take it. I'll start a new one tomorrow, with my ears washed out.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Oh. Mind the needles, they get everywhere. I'm Tamsin. I knit.
This is a headband for the hare by the road head. His ears go flat with cold.
I've never measured him. I didn't like to ask. So it might not fit at all.

choices.text: how will you know it fits?

speaker: tamsin
lines: Walk up to a hare and ask him to hold still while I measure his ears? I'd sooner knit in the dark.
So I guess. I always guess. Would you help me find out if I guessed right?

speaker: tamsin
lines: He lives by the road head, in Hearth Hollow. Hollis, he's called.
Take it to him and ask him to try it on. I'd only fret.
And have a go at the pinecone toss while you're here, if you like. I like watching someone else be bad at something.
Then come back and tell me if it fits. Honestly. I'd rather know.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Still got it? Hollis, the hare by the road head. Ask him to try it on.
If it's too tight, tell me true. I'd rather know.

speaker: tamsin
lines: It fits? Tight on the ears, but it fits? Oh, thank goodness.
Then the next one gets more room round the ears. Keep this one. It was practice.
And next time I'll ask him myself. Out loud.

speaker: fen
lines: You're up early. Or late. Hard to tell from a pine.
I watch the pines. Everything that moves through here goes in my tally. Nearly everything.

speaker: fen
lines: The wood is all comings and goings. Somebody should keep track. It isn't prying if you write it down.
Most folk talk around an owl, hoping he'll fill in the rest. I don't.

speaker: fen
lines: From this branch I see the creek. Up the hill there's a deer trail, and the trees hide it from me.
Something goes down that trail every day. I see it go in at the top. I never see what it is.
Run the trail, fast, and you'll see where it bends: past the glade and the split pine.
Tamsin, the marten who knits by the split pine, sits at the bend. Ask her what comes past.

speaker: fen
lines: You're back. Run the deer trail, fast. See where it bends.
Then ask Tamsin, by the split pine, what comes down it. Then tell me.

speaker: fen
lines: The deer trail first, fast. Then Tamsin, by the split pine. She sees what comes past.

speaker: fen
lines: A roe deer? From the glade, down to drink at the creek, every morning?
There. That's the last line in the tally.
Twenty winters I've watched this wood. I could have asked the marten next door any day.

speaker: ilsa
lines: You're Pip. Nana's told me about you. Don't stand still, you'll freeze.
I'm Ilsa. I carry things. Firewood, parcels, whatever wants carrying.
This one's for my sister. We had words, and I'd rather not be the one to carry it over.

speaker: ilsa
lines: She says I carry everyone's load and then sulk that nobody carries mine.
I say she sits in her steam and waits for people to come to her.
We're both right. That's the worst way to have a row.

speaker: ilsa
lines: My sister Ivy keeps the hot pools at Kettle Springs, down the valley.
Put it in her hands, not on the step. She'll say I should have come myself.
Don't argue with her. Just come back and tell me it landed.

speaker: ilsa
lines: Still carrying it? Good. Ivy, my sister, is at the pools, in the steam.
If she starts, don't argue. Hand it over and say it's from me.

speaker: ilsa
lines: It landed? She took it?
And she said to come down myself. Of course she did.
Then tomorrow I'll go down. Carrying nothing. I'll let her feed me.
Sit a minute first. No, sit. I'm practising.

speaker: fen
lines: You asked me straight out. Hardly anyone does. Most hint and hope.
I saw it. Hollis, the hare, hung it on a low branch to dry.
Wind took it into the creek pool below the split pine. The pine with two tops, standing over the rest, a short walk up the creek from my branch. Fish there and you'll hook it.
I didn't take it. Tell him that. He's been thinking it for two days.

speaker: tamsin
lines: Fen, the owl, wants to know what uses the deer trail? He could have asked me.
It's the roe deer from the hoarfrost glade. She comes past my stump every morning, down to the creek to drink.
Tell him that. And tell him he's allowed to come and ask himself.

speaker: wren
lines: I've started a new book. I write slower now. I listen longer first.
Listen. That knocking is the pines in the cold. I'd stopped hearing it.
If you hear something I haven't, come and tell me. I'll write it down.

speaker: tamsin
lines: I'm knitting another. Measured, this time. I asked the hare to hold still, and he did.
Turns out people like being asked. Who knew.
Mind the needles on the stump. They're sharper than they look.

speaker: fen
lines: The tally's whole. A roe deer, every morning, down to the creek.
I asked the marten by the split pine something yesterday. She talked for an hour. I may do it again.
Ask me something, if you like. I answer when I'm asked.

speaker: ilsa
lines: Tomorrow I'm going down to Ivy, my sister. I'll let her feed me.
Don't tell her. She'll make a row of it, and I'll secretly enjoy it.
Sit a while. I'm practising sitting. I'm not much good at it yet.
